rows.description: Hiding EMIs and credit card dues from family adds isolation. Face the actual numbers on paper, prioritise high-interest debt, and tell one trusted person. Shame keeps debts growing.

You took a loan partly to support family expectations, and now feel trapped between duty and survival. Talk openly with them about limits, set a repayment plan, and avoid pretending to be richer than you are.
Easy credit, buy-now-pay-later and status spending feel harmless. Track small EMIs, ask if the item is a need, and delay purchases for a week. Debt for lifestyle steals future freedom.
You lent a friend money and they keep dodging you. You feel used. Ask once, clearly, propose a plan, and decide how much of the friendship you value. Lend only what you can afford to lose.

I fear that the other side's victory will destroy what I value. The fear is sincere. Wise: check facts from varied sources, notice when fear is being sold to me, and act through voting and local work. Harmful: seeing all opponents as enemies.
Asks "how did you come to that view?" and finds shared values beneath disagreement.
I admire a political leader and feel proud when he speaks. Wise: support policies on evidence, and stay able to criticise my own side. Harmful: treating criticism of the leader as an attack on me.

A relative at a family dinner shouts that my views are "brainwashed". I feel insulted and want to retaliate. Wise: decline to debate while heated, say it calmly, and change the subject. Harmful: escalating until dinner is ruined.
I want to hit back with something equally cruel. Wise: the impulse is human, but revenge often makes things worse; choose evidence and reporting.
I dread going to school because of what's online. Wise: fear is a signal, not weakness; tell a parent or counsellor, and request the school to act.
An anonymous account sends nasty messages and I obsess over who it is. Wise: preserve evidence, report to platform and school, and don't let guessing consume me.
Classmates post memes or edited photos to mock me. I feel hurt and exposed. Wise: don't retaliate, save screenshots, block, report, and tell a trusted adult; it is not my fault.
After being lied to many times, you trust no news at all. Total distrust is as manipulable as blind trust. Keep a small set of sources with track records of corrections, and hold conclusions loosely.

Campaigns use edited clips and fear-based rumours to steer emotion. Notice who benefits, check multiple sources, and be cautious about content that flatters your side. Media literacy is a civic skill.

Your feed keeps you angry and hooked, and you notice worse mood and warped views. Curate sources, schedule offline time, read long-form, and remember outrage is what platforms reward. You are shaping your mind with your attention.

You shared something false and it caused panic or hurt someone. Delete it, post a correction to the same audience, and apologise if named. Building the habit of checking before sharing repairs more than shame does.

My mum's new partner tries to be friendly and I refuse. I fear he will replace my dad. It is fine to go slowly. I stay polite, be honest about feelings, and let trust grow without being forced to love.
When my parents separate, I miss the old family and cry at odd times. Grief is normal even though nobody died. I keep routines, talk about it, and let myself be sad without hurrying to be okay.
I keep hoping they will get back together and imagine plans to fix it. This is common, but I cannot fix their marriage. Accepting slowly frees me to enjoy time with each parent as it is.

I am angry at both of them for ruining our home. Anger covers sadness. Wise: say it in words, maybe draw or run. Slamming doors is natural, but hurting others or blaming one parent unfairly will hurt me more.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: You explore new customs, foods and ways of working with interest. Adapt where it helps and stay rooted where it matters. Learning does not mean betraying your own culture or copying blindly.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: You face stereotypes, accent mockery or being left out. It hurts and can shake confidence. Name it to yourself, find supportive people, address it calmly when safe, and report discrimination. Their bias is not your defect.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: You live far from ageing parents and feel torn between career and duty. Set regular calls, plan visits, arrange local support, and be honest about limits. Guilt without action helps no one, and love can travel.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: In a new city or country, you miss home food, language and easy jokes. Loneliness is normal at first. Join clubs, meet colleagues outside work, keep calls with family, and give yourself months, not weeks, to belong.
